I believe one of the most important actions you should do is probably record a conversation with him. Mainly because one of the first things we often forget when a person passes is the sound of their voice.

"Where is the will?"

I'm not being facetious. My dad died abruptly of lung cancer and I never got to ask him, well, anything (it advanced so rapidly that by the time I knew anything, he was already in ICU and too fucked up to communicate). I had no fucking clue what I was supposed to do with his house or his responsibilities to other people (things he had a hand in, like being the archivist for one small national group, as a hobby). I didn't know what bills to pay--he had gone entirely paperless, so nothing came in the regular mail, and I didn't have the password to his email. We didn't find out about his IRA until something like 7 years later--after the bank with the account didn't hear from him for literally many years, they finally sent a paper mail, which went through the new owners and some town lawyer and eventually got to me.

So, nail down all the practical stuff. "Is there a will, is there anything I need to handle or wrap up, who do I contact?" Seriously, I ended up just going through his address book and calling everyone, having no idea which were his friends and which were people he only knew professionally or had only spoken to a few times. One entry turned out to be the wrong guy completely, that phone call was a farce. He was in the shower in the first place, so I gave his wife the message to give to him, and he called me back saying he was really sorry to hear my dad died but he had no idea who my dad was and had never spoken to him.

Once you make sure you've nailed down the practical/logistical stuff... well... I mean first, I'd ask, is there anything you'd planned to tell me eventually and hadn't gotten around to--like, I don't know, stuff that was going on during your childhood that he didn't tell you about, but that you might find interesting. Quirks about your mother or other relatives which would be in your interest to finally learn about. Turned out my dad had a lot of shit like this but I found it out by going through all the boxes of old letters he had in the basement. There was a lot of shit I would have needed to talk to him about, had I ever known about it while he was alive.

To help clarify, an example: it turned out he'd had exactly the same relationship dysfunctions I did--very serious ones, which led to two incredibly shitty marriages for him--but when I'd been going through it myself, with girlfriends, he would listen to me but never seemed to relate to anything I was describing. I really would have wanted to say, "...you did this too? This is so different from who you are now--can you tell me about how it changed you, did you give up on relationships completely? You've always seemed to have this kind of emotional numbness, but in the pictures from that time you look so alive... and this is so much like what I've just gone through... why did you never say you know exactly what it's like because you did the same thing repeatedly? Do you think there's no solution other than to give up?"

There was stuff about his childhood which, though he never lied about any of it (as far as I can tell), the picture looked pretty different after I learned some other people's perspectives on it. He was a very insightful and intelligent guy, and though he had as many blind spots as anyone, he had a greater than average ability and willingness to examine them--I would have wanted to ask him if he thought any of his worldview was somewhat sour-grapes because of rejection, and if there was anything he wanted to reconsider in that light.

If he had enough time and energy--if the cancer wasn't that far yet--I'd ask if he was willing to put together an autobiography, with my help. (His own mother did that--it was only something like a dozen pages long, but it was a small treasure to us, especially the descriptions of her childhood, so long ago and so rural as to seem alien.)

I'd ask if there was anything he wanted to tell me about ways I was screwing myself in the long term--like, with a lot of people, you can see there's some habit they have that's hurting them and which they seem blind to, but you never bring it up because you know they're not going to change it, because it's so ingrained and they have such strong defenses/justifications for it. I'd ask him if he could point out mine. I wouldn't have to be ready to accept/believe them on the spot, and he could be honest knowing there was no threat to our future relationship even if it upset me; I'd have years to try to come to terms with whatever it was.

When my grandfather died (a true story teller in his own right) and no one bothered to record a single thing from him, I felt like I'd lost a lot more than my grandpa. I lost his stories. After that, I got older and camcorders became a thing. I decided to record my family starting from the oldest, to my parents and aunts and uncles. I composed a list of questions that I'd ask every one of them. These are used as cues to get them remembering something. When they say something interesting, don't hesitate to ask them to expand on it. I have an uncle that filled up six 8mm cassettes with stories of Alaska that could be used for an amazing movie script. He's been dead for five years now, but I have his smiles, his laughs, his stories, and watching those videos means the world to me. Here's the list of questions I ask in my interviews. Feel free to expand on them as needed, but make sure you videotape the whole thing. Make sure you have good lighting and good sound quality. Twenty years from now, you'll watch your videos and be thankful you took the time.

  1. Tell me a little about yourself (name, birthplace)

  2. Tell me about your parents.

  3. Tell me about where you went to school.

  4. What is your favorite memory of your school days?

  5. Who was the biggest influence on you as a child? Why?

  6. First boyfriend / girlfriend

  7. How did you meet your husband / wife (if applicable)

  8. Favorite memory of your mother.

  9. Favorite memory of your father.

  10. Where were you when JFK died (you heard about 9/11)?

  11. What did you think of man landing on the moon (Mt. St. Helens erupting)?

  12. Where is the farthest place you’ve been to where you live now?

  13. What year did you move into the house you live in now?

  14. How much did you pay for it (rent)? Any renovations?

  15. Any trouble financing the house?

  16. Go into detail about your immediate family.

  17. What jobs have you had, and which was your favorite?

  18. What community service have you done, if any?

  19. Who was your favorite singer when you were in high school?

  20. Favorite actor / actress in high school?

  21. If you could go anywhere in the world, where would you go? Why?

  22. If you won the lottery, what would you do with it?

  23. What advice would you give your great, great, grandchildren?

  24. If you could spend one day with a famous person whether they are alive today or not, who would it be? Why?

  25. (If old enough to have experienced JFK) Where were you on 9/11/01?

  26. Tell me a story about someone important to you.

  27. What is one thing you want, but don’t have?

  28. Tell me a story from your childhood.

  29. Tell me one thing you wish you could change about yourself and why?

  30. If you had to give up one modern convenience, what would it be?

  31. What is one thing you wish you knew more about?

  32. Describe your dream house.

  33. Tell me about the best vacation you’ve been on.

  34. If you were offered a chance to live as they did in the 1700’s, would you do it? What would be your motivation?

  35. Tell me a story about something you got away with as a kid.

  36. What did you want to be growing up?

  37. Tell me about something that makes you happy.

  38. Open forum (you can say or discuss anything you’d like at this point)

My dad was born in Russia in 1937 and fled across Europe during WWII. Growing up, I always heard stories about this, but he was always a little uncomfortable talking about parts of it, and I never really got the whole story from start to finish. A few years ago, I was visiting him over a weekend (he lived about 3 hours away) and asked if he'd be willing to sit down with me and an audio recorder and tell me everything he could remember. To my surprise, he agreed and I made a mental note to bring down the stuff with me the next time I came to visit.

The very next weekend, he was hiking in the woods near his house and disturbed a bee's nest. Whether from an allergic reaction or the exertion of running away, he lost consciousness and suffered an anoxic brain injury. He lived another 6 months or so, but had some pretty serious brain damage. On the bright side, I got to tell him I loved him before he died. But not learning his story is one of the greatest regrets I have in life.

FWIW, I'm sorry you're going through this OP. I know it sucks. I hope you can find peace with your dad.
